answer.sourceLine: Jordan really said it, in the closing seconds of his Basketball Hall of Fame enshrinement address at Symphony Hall in Springfield, Massachusetts, on 11 September 2009. He delivered it as two sentences — “Never say never. Because limits, like fears, are often just an illusion.” — and the popular single-sentence version simply swaps that full stop for a comma; no words are added, dropped or reordered.

author.name: Michael Jordan
author.heading: Who was Michael Jordan?
author.metaLine: Born 17 February 1963 · American basketball player · Hall of Fame Class of 2009
author.bio: Michael Jeffrey Jordan, born 17 February 1963 in Brooklyn, New York, played fifteen NBA seasons for the Chicago Bulls and the Washington Wizards, winning six championships in Chicago. He was enshrined in the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame with the Class of 2009. His induction speech is remembered less for gratitude than for grievance — he used it to relitigate old slights — which is why the one genuinely uplifting line in it, the last one, travelled so far on its own.

misattribution.heading: The name is right. The punctuation isn’t.
misattribution.intro: This is the rare famous-athlete quote that survives checking. What has drifted is not the attribution but the shape of the sentence — and, on one branch of the family tree, the grammar.

items.why: Jordan spoke two sentences with a clear stop between them: “Never say never. Because limits, like fears, are often just an illusion.” ↗ The comma-joined form is a tidy-up, not a fabrication — the words and their order are untouched, and ESPN was already printing the merged version in September 2009.

items.who: “Limits, like fear, is often an illusion”
items.why: A singular, ungrammatical variant that still circulates on aggregator sites. It traces to the Chicago Bulls’ own NBA.com column on the speech ↗, which quoted the closing loosely inside a report rather than reproducing a transcript.

items.who: Quote sites that give no source at all
items.why: Most pages carrying this line name only “Michael Jordan,” with no speech, venue or date — the same treatment they give the fabricated lines pinned on him. The provenance is a matter of record: the closing of the Hall of Fame enshrinement address ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuine Jordan, spoken 11 September 2009 at Symphony Hall in Springfield, Massachusetts, and confirmed by Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗ as well as two independent transcripts.

context.heading: Why he said it
lead: Jordan’s enshrinement speech ran far past its allotted time and startled the room. He cried, then spent much of the address settling scores — with the coach who cut him in high school, with executives, with rivals who had doubted him. The last thirty seconds swerved. He turned to what the game had meant to him, called it his refuge, and then, half-joking, floated a comeback: “One day you might look up and see me playing the game at 50.”

The audience laughed. He told them not to, and delivered the line, leaving the stage on a thank-you seconds later. Read cold it is a motivational poster; read in place it is the same competitive needle that powered the rest of the speech, aimed one last time at anyone in the hall who assumed he was finished. He never did play at 50.
context.detailsSummary: A note on the two versions
detailsBody: The wording you see on quote sites splits into two families. The dominant one — “Never say never, because limits, like fears, are often just an illusion” — matches the full transcripts and is what ESPN printed in September 2009. A second, mangled family reads “Limits, like fear, is often an illusion,” singular and ungrammatical; that phrasing traces to the same-night write-up on the Chicago Bulls’ NBA.com site, which transcribed the line loosely inside a column rather than a transcript.
context.pull: He was not writing a slogan. He was refusing, on the way out the door, to concede that anything was over.
